title: Read-After-Write Consistency Across Database Replicas: Overcoming Replication Lag with Log Sequence Numbers
summary: Scaling database architectures typically involves directing all writes to a primary node and distributing read queries across a fleet of asynchronous read replicas. However, asynchronous replication inherently introduces replication lag. When a user posts a comment and immediately refreshes the page, the read query frequently hits a replica that has not yet ingested the write, causing the user's new comment to disappear. Ensuring read-after-write consistency without overloading the primary database requires tracking replication Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs) and session-level causality routing.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Telegram Dispatcher and the Newspaper Editions
analogy:
Imagine publishing a breaking news bulletin at a newspaper headquarters.

Under Blind Replica Routing (The Delayed Newspaper), you submit a correction to the editor (Primary Node) at 2:00 PM. The editor publishes it in Edition #402. You walk out to a street kiosk (Read Replica #3) at 2:01 PM and buy a paper, but the kiosk is still selling Edition #401 delivered 10 minutes ago. Your correction is missing, so you panic thinking the editor deleted your story.

Under LSN-Aware Causality Routing (The Edition Check Stamp), the editor stamps your receipt with 'Edition #402'. When you approach the street kiosk, you show your stamp. If the kiosk is only on Edition #401, the vendor either asks you to wait 2 seconds while the delivery truck arrives, or directs you to the central office newsroom where Edition #402 is already live, guaranteeing you never see an outdated world.

sections.heading: 1. The Anatomy of Replication Lag and Ghost Data
sections.content:
In high-throughput databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL, writes commit to the primary Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and are shipped asynchronously over the network to read replicas.

• The Replication Delay Gap: Network jitter, disk I/O contention, or long-running analytical queries on replicas can cause replication lag to fluctuate between 50 milliseconds and several minutes.
• The User Experience Disaster: If a user updates their profile picture and the subsequent HTTP GET request routes to a lagged replica, the old avatar appears. Users assume their update failed and repeatedly hammer the save button, generating cascading write traffic.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Mitigation Strategies: From Naive to State-of-the-Art
sections.content:
Engineering teams employ several patterns to restore consistency:

• 1. Naive Primary Pinning (Anti-Pattern): Routing all reads for logged-in users to the primary defeats the purpose of horizontal read scaling, quickly exhausting primary database connection pools.
• 2. Time-Window Sticky Routing: After any write, a user session is flagged in Redis to route reads to the primary for 5 seconds. While simple, it sends excessive read traffic to the primary during bursts and fails when replication lag spikes beyond 5 seconds.
• 3. Synchronous Replication (High Latency): Forcing the primary to wait for quorum acknowledgment on every write guarantees zero lag on replicas, but spikes write latency by cross-node network round-trips and risks total write stalls if replicas fail.

sections.heading: 3. The Production Standard: LSN-Based Causal Tracking
sections.content:
Modern distributed architectures (like GitHub and Shopify) use database Log Sequence Numbers (LSN) or Global Transaction Identifiers (GTID):

• WAL LSN Extraction: When a write transaction commits on the primary, PostgreSQL returns the current commit LSN via pg_current_wal_lsn() (e.g., 0/16B3748).
• Session Token Encoding: The application server attaches this LSN to the client's session cookie or JWT: X-Min-LSN: 0/16B3748.
• Replica Readiness Check: On subsequent read requests, the router queries the candidate replica's replay position: pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(). If the replica's replayed LSN ≥ the session's required LSN, the read executes locally. If the replica is behind, the query either blocks briefly for catch-up (bounded by 50ms) or routes to the primary as a fallback.

takeaway: Asynchronous replication lag causes newly written data to disappear when immediate reads land on stale replicas. Modern architectures extract the Write-Ahead Log sequence number (LSN) during commits and route reads only to replicas whose replay position meets or exceeds that LSN, guaranteeing causal consistency without pinning reads to the primary.
